hello everyone and welcome to this video in this video i'm going to walk you through the master class outline so let's go ahead and get started so i included the master class outline which is this excel sheet as part of the course package so in module one we're gonna start with an introduction to the master class and cover the key success tips to get the best out of this course we're also going to cover a quick demo as well of how to use cloud code and cloud co-work in module two we are going to focus primarily on cloud co-work so we're going to cover the fundamentals of how to use cloud co-work to make changes directly inside of folders on your computer so we'll learn how to create excel sheets how to build powerpoint presentations how to do research as well and also we're going to cover what we call it cloud skills plugins and model context protocol or mcp for short we're also going to use existing plugins so anthropic which is the company that created cloud they did a great job of creating multiple plugins so now you have a finance plugin you have a marketing you have legal and so on so i'm going to show you kind of how to use existing plugins i'm going to learn how to do financial forecasting

as well with one of these plugins we'll also learn how to create our own plugin as well please note that there's a lot of content here i just want to give you a quick overview of what we're going to cover and then of course in every single module we're going to have a lot of practice opportunities so we are going to learn by doing and finally we're going to use cloud co-work to perform multitasking so we're going to use these agents to perform deep research to combine the results to create powerpoint presentations and also create pdfs as well in module three we are going to shift gears from cloud co-work and we're going to shift to cloud chat this should be an easy section i would say so we'll learn how to do prompt engineering i'm going to cover all the key success tips as well when you are drafting your prompt afterwards we're going to use cloud for content creation for code generation for learning new topics we're also going to use it for image recognition and problem solving and finally we're going to use what we call a plan with cloud so we're going to use cloud to work with it basically as a planning partner so we're going to use it for coding learning and writing as well in module 4 we're going to use cloud inside of excel so

going to write a single line of code and we're going to learn how to build a functioning app and also improve its design as well with the front end design skill afterwards in module 8 i'm going to show you how to build ai agents with the power of cloud code so think of it as if you wanted to automate part of your business now you can use cloud code to do that so we're going to cover all the ai agents frameworks how to do multi-agents and sub-agents we're going to learn how to build ai agents with tools with memory and also build a team of ai agents without writing a single line of code and that simply is the outline for this master class you're going to learn a lot i'm super excited to get started so that's all i have for this video i hope you enjoyed it and see you in the next one

lectures.title: Introduction to Claude Cowork
lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this module. In this module, we are going to master Cloud Co-Work. So let's go ahead and get started. So we're going to start with the module introduction, and we're going to cover the key learning objectives of this entire section of this course. So here is the module agenda. First, we're going to start with an introduction to Cloud Co-Work. And if you haven't used Cloud Co-Work, it is an incredible tool that goes beyond just using a regular chat bot.

So what we used to do before, let's say if you have interacted with chat GPT or maybe here with Cloud Chat, you simply had a box, and you just type your prompt, kind of what you want from AI in plain English. And then what we used to get is just getting a feedback, and that's it. What's happening right now is with Cloud Co-Work, now you can direct these AI agents directly to work in a folder. So for example, now I can direct it to, let's say, a folder that includes some of my financial data.

And now this AI agent is going to create its own tasks. It is going to perform an action directly inside my folder, which is, think of it as mind-blowing. What you could do as well, which is what Anthropic recently released. So Anthropic is the company that created Cloud. And now you can basically give it a command just using your phone. So I'm going to show you as well later on, which is going to be mind-blowing, is now you can have your phone.

You can just even talk to it just in plain English, and it's going to create the financial model for me. And now Cloud Co-Work is going to go ahead and build it for you, which is insane. OK, so first we're going to start with an introduction to Cloud Co-Work. So we're going to start with an overview. We're going to cover the core concepts and how what we call it skills and plugins and connectors play a key role in there. We're also going to cover the Cloud Co-Work ecosystem.

Basically, what makes Cloud specifically unique compared to other AI models providers is now you have the ability to add a skill. lectures.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Connectors
lectures.text:
Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video I'm going to share an important protocol known as MCP or Model Context Protocol. So let's go ahead and get started. So what is Model Context Protocol? So in order for the AI agents, let's say like Claude Cowork for example, to connect to other tools like let's say Gmail or maybe connecting to Teams, basically they need a standardized way to talk to all these tools and that's where MCP comes into play or Model Context Protocol. I know it sounds a bit intimidating or fancy, really what it is, it is just a standard way for the agents to talk to the outside world. So MCP is a standard open source framework that was actually developed by Anthropic, which is the same company that developed Claude or Claude Cowork as well of course, to standardize how artificial intelligence models and agents interact with external tools, systems, and data sources.

This is what Model Context Protocol logo looks like and what we do kind of as an analogy is well we say okay like MCP, think of it as the standardized USB-C port for example. Think of it as with USB-C, you can just take that and you can just plug it really anywhere that uses USB-C and it should work. And that's the idea here of Model Context Protocol. You have a tool, this could be Gmail, it's just that tool says okay I support MCP, this is great. Now me as an AI agent, I can go and talk to it easily with a standardized way. So before MCP, which is what we had here on the left hand side, it was a mess. We had an AI agent which could be powered by open AI, GPT models, or LLAMA, let's say open source models, or even Claude here. And let's say these agents or LLMs, they come from different providers and they actually wanted to talk to different services like Gmail, like Slack, like Google Calendar. What we used to do before, which is thank God we don't have to do it again, we have to create custom APIs, like custom way to talk to all of these. And the problem is maybe Slack decided to release a new version for example, or maybe a new tool or something along those lines. And now you need to go back and update

that code. And that's what we used to do before. But now the solution is, well, please use MCP or Model Context Protocol. And now I got the AI agent here. Here I got all these different tools or services. And now I got a standardized way or a standardized protocol to talk to all of these. So now I can connect that MCP or talk to it, of course, using that kind of metaphor, which is the USB-C stick. And now I'm able to talk to all of these services using a standardized API.

Okay. So please note that when you open Claude co-work, you have the ability to connect to many tools and services available out there. We call them connectors using MCP. So connectors let Claude pull from external sources. So for example, if I would like to analyze, let's say a Google Sheet, then move a chart directly into a PowerPoint deck. So now this agent can basically talk to all of these different tools and services easily with the power of MCP. There are a ton of connectors available inside of Claude co-work. So you can connect it to Google Drive, you can connect it to your email to manage your calendar, and also connect it to Gmail, Slack, and many, many more as well. So what I've done here is I included a link to the documentation for MCP.

So let me show you. So this is simply, so if you go to that link, now we should see Anthropic basically introducing that model context protocol or MCP here. And it's actually quite new still, that was like, it was released in November 25 of 2024, like year 2024. And you should see the description here of what MCP is, how does it work, and so on. And it's also open source that which is really smart move by Anthropic because it became a standard across all pretty much LLMs of large language models providers as well. Okay, so let me show you a practical application for MCP or model context protocol. Assume that here I got an AI agent, and that AI agent would like to utilize a currency converter. This currency converter is running here, okay, and it's actually running on an MCP server. Think of it again, it's a server that supports that MCP or model context protocol to be running on it. So here I got that tool, and here I got me as a client. The client is going to ask an LLM or let's say an AI agent a question, what is 1000 US dollars in Canadian terms?

What the LLM or the agent is going to do is going to use model context protocol to invoke or talk to this tool here using MCP. And because this tool is supporting MCP as well, now it should be able to again plug and play. And now they can talk to each other easily. Again, as I mentioned here, MCP is an open protocol designed to be a standardized way for models to discover and interact with tools. Think of it again, it's like a universal plug adapter for AI tools.

And what you get at the end back, you get well, the equivalent Canadian dollars, which is let's say 1000 USD becomes 1370 Canadian dollars, for example. So the agent will use MCP or model context protocol, which is a standardized protocol that connects LLMs and agents to various external tools and data sources as well. With that, that's all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it. Now let's shift back to cloud co-work and show you how you can connect cloud to various connectors like Gmail, for example. I hope you enjoyed this video and see you in the next one.

lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. In this video, I'm going to cover the fundamentals of prompt engineering. So let's go ahead and get started. Please note that we are going to cover this topic here because over the next few videos, I'm going to show you how we're going to structure the prompt in a specific format to maximize the output that we get from our large language models and specifically from Cloud. So what is prompt engineering?

Well, prompt engineering is the practice of designing and optimizing text input to generative AI models to obtain desired responses. Think of it as the art of talking to these AI models. For example, you can ask these AI models to recommend a book for you. Of course, this is too vague, too generic. We try to avoid prompting these AI models with this technique. What we try to do is we try to be more specific. So we can say, I want you to recommend a fiction book, which is slightly better.

So now the AI model will know your intent slightly better. So that means the output that you expect from them should be enhanced. Or you can be ultra-specific. So you can say, I want you to recommend a historical fiction book set in World War II. So by going from top here to the bottom, now you are improving the quality of the prompt so you can guide the AI model, specifically Cloud, to generate better outputs. Okay, so to structure any prompt, we usually divide them into four components.

The first one is what we call it context. Think of it as we try to set the scene to the AI model so it basically knows what is going on, like who am I as a person, let's say. So for example, you can tell the AI here, you are a smart home energy advisor who helps homeowners reduce energy costs. This is the context. You can tell AI models, for example, that you are a data scientist or maybe you are a PhD researcher. And that's actually one of the examples that we're going to cover in the next video.

So this is the first part of the prompt. Second, we give it clear instructions, simply a clear statement of the desired goal. For example, I can say, when given a household prompt, I want you to provide practical, prioritized advice. Think of it as you are onboarding a new employee. You want to tell them, okay, what your job is, right, kind of background information. And then you tell this new employee clear instructions of what you want them to do.

And these are the two core components of any prompt. The third part is you can also give it input data, and this is optional. This is the data or content to analyze. So for example, I can say you will receive a question about energy usage or device efficiency. And please know that this is optional. At least you need to have the context and the instruction as well. Finally, the fourth part is what we call it output indicator. Think of it as, okay, these AI models are going to generate something, right?

It could be data analysis, or maybe it could be a PowerPoint presentation, or maybe an Excel sheet, for example. So here, what we're doing is we're going to define the expected format and structure of the output. For example, you can say respond with a short, clear recommendation list, let's say two to four bullet points, one quick win that can be done today. For example, if you're asking these AI models to generate a research report, in the output indicator, you can clearly mention that.

You can mention, I want you to generate a full report, and these are the sections of the report. I need to have background information. I need to have, let's say, resources in the appendix, and so on. So these, I would say, are the four core components of prompts. So when it comes to prompting essentials, here are the top tips or success tips. The first one is to guide the behavior with system prompt. So as I mentioned before, you can actually tell these AI models basically who you are as a person, so you can get them a persona, you specify the rules, and also constraints, and also what the output should look like as well.

Force the model to avoid hallucinations. So especially if you're working with sensitive information, like let's say you work in finance, and you're asking these AI models to, let's say, extract financial data from 10K reports. So what you could do is you can tell these LLMs, or Claude specifically here in this example, don't hallucinate. Ground your results in the provided data. If data is missing, say not enough info instead of guessing. And by doing that, we found that these AI models can actually reduce their creative aspects.

So these LLMs can get really creative. Basically, think of it as it's a parameter inside these LLMs. We call it temperature. So if you increase the temperature, these models become super creative. But if you reduce this temperature, these models are going to be more factual. You're not going to get creative. So you can mention that in the prompt. And we found that just by saying that as part of the prompt, the response or the performance of these AI models actually improve quite a bit, unless you're looking for a creative output.

That's a different story, of course. Next, you can ask for reasoning or chain of thought. For example, you can tell these AI models as part of your prompts, I want you to explain your steps. I want you to show the calculations before the results. That will allow you to build trust and transparency in these models. Next, you can also tell it to add constraints and boundaries, meaning in the output, for example. I'm going to tell it, I want you to explain the output in three bullet points, max 15 words each.

And now these AI models are going to know its constraints and it's going to know the boundaries. I can tell it, for example, I don't want you to talk anything politics. And that will be part of the guardrails that you add to these LLMs or agents. Next is iterate and refine. So the first draft is rarely final. We actually go through multiple iterations to improve these prompts, tweak the wording, add details, narrow scope, and the output basically simply finally clicks.

And then what we do too is we anchor with examples, and that's what we call it few-shot prompting. So let's assume that you spoke to Claude and the Claude didn't understand what you mean. So what you could do is as part of the prompt, as part of the input to these LLMs, you can actually tell it what's good looks like for us humans. For example, I can explain to it in detail, this is what I'm looking for as an example. You can also include screenshots as well of the good answer in your eyes.

And now these AI models are going to follow your lead. So try to be the boss and try to manage these LLMs, especially agents, by giving them more details and also anchoring with examples as well. Please note that here, we usually try to avoid using examples in the prompt itself unless you need it, because when you do that, you are actually consuming a lot of tokens in the input. Finally, you can also tell these AI models to generate structured output.

So you can say, for example, the output could be in a JSON format or maybe a text format and so on. And that's pretty much all I want you to know when it comes to prompt engineering and also the top key essentials when it comes to prompting. In the next video, I'm going to show you a few additional prompting techniques, and then we're going to go back and we'll get started with our practical demo. I hope you enjoyed this video and see you in the next one.

Let me show you a practical example Let's assume that you would like to acquire a business In order for us to value that business What we do is we take a look at the free cash flow of that business in the future Like next year in year two year three and so on and then what we do is we discount all these cash flow to the present and

Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video I'm going to share from a very high level what do we mean by a leveraged buyout and the idea that we wanted to use Claude to build our financial models but in this video I just wanted to share what is actually going on behind the scenes and then in the next video I'm going to show you how Claude can automate the entire process for building and validating as well these financial models. So let's go ahead and get started. So what is a leveraged buyout? Well an LBO or a leveraged buyout is when a company is purchased using a combination of equity like cash from investors and large amount of debt as well and of course they're going to be borrowed money. So the key idea here is that the assets and cash flows of the company being acquired are often used as collateral to secure and repay the borrowed funds. So let me show you that visually. Let's assume that you are a buyer let's say Blackstone for example and here you have a target company this company is called Cardinal Health and let's assume that this company has strong potential like you think you can acquire this company and maybe in four or five years just make it grow and then now you can sell it okay

so what you could do here is well you are going to involve a bank let's say a lender for example JP Morgan Chase and the idea here is very simple as a private equity firm as a buyer you're gonna go you're going to get a loan from the bank right and that loan is going to be of let's say the majority of the of the deal let's say it's 80 percent and what you're going to do is you're going to take that money and you're going to put money as well you know as equity or cash from investors too so you have the deal is structured kind of in both parts you have lended money from the bank which is what we got here and you also invested let's say 20 percent as well and the buyer which is Blackstone is going to use debt and equity to acquire a target company which is let's say Cardinal Health you're going to take that company and then the acquired companies operating cash flow so these companies they're going to basically make it grow it's going to generate more cash flows possibly it's going to generate profit and then we're going to use that operating cash flow to service the debt to the bank and that's the idea and after a few years you can sell it and maybe make like you know like 40 percent return let's say per year

or something along those lines so these are the steps for a leverage buyout simply first you identify a target company an investor or a private equity firm finds a company they want to buy and then what they do they secure debt financing so they borrow a significant portion of the purchase price from the bank and then they also put equity in it right so they put actually cash as well in it the investor also invests some of their own money it's going to be a smaller portion compared to the debt that they took from the bank and then they acquire the company so they use both debt and equity to make that purchase and finally they repay debt so over time the company's future profits and cash flows are going to be used to pay off that debt or that loan and let's take a look at the practical example that we are going to ask Claude to build it for us I'm going to say Blackstone is evaluating the potential leverage buyout of Cardinal Health which is this company here with financing support from JPMorgan Chase so again this is a private equity firm you have a bank the lender right and you have the target company that you wanted to acquire Blackstone plans you to use of course a combination of debt loan from JPMorgan and equity

as well to acquire the company and then estimate investor returns based on the projected performance with an exit strategy after five years these are simply the assumptions that we are going to feed to Claude to build our financial model we're going to say the purchase price is let's say 100 million dollars the debt is going to be 70 million the investors money let's say the equity is going to be 30 million like 30 percent of the deal the EBITDA at year one is going to be 20 million with growth by two percent every year the debt interest rate is going to be 10 percent the annual debt repayment 10 million and that's pretty much it for all the assumptions and that's all I have for this video I hope you enjoyed it it's just a quick overview video please if you are not from a finance background or maybe you didn't fully get what is going on really all what we're doing is we wanted to ask Claude to build the financial model for us and I'm going to show you the prompt you can just feed it to prompt to Claude and then it should work quite well and the objective is just to show you the power of using Claude to build real world financial models that are quite advanced with that that's all I have for this video I hope you enjoyed it and see you in the next one

So the idea is you can ask Cloud Code to build applications for you. You can ask it to build landing pages. You can also install a skill. So now Cloud Code will have some sort of superpowers. And instead of having one coding agent running your code, now you can have a team of agents and sub-agents that can go, they can read your code base, and now they can make edits. You can also plan as well with Cloud.

And when I started to use Cloud Code maybe like a year ago or so, I would say like with the latest model, which is Opus 4.6 model, the capabilities became incredibly powerful. And I speak to a lot of developers pretty much at a lot of frontier labs, and they tell you that almost like 90% of the code that they write is actually developed by Cloud Code, which is insane. So Cloud Code is available in the terminal, in VS Code, in Antigravity, and also it is available in the Cloud Desktop app. In this course, we are going to use VS Code. So Cloud Code allows you to read and write code, so it can analyze your entire code base, makes targeted edits, and creates new files as well. It also allows you to run commands, so it can execute shell commands, run tests, manage Git, and builds projects for you. And then finally, you will be able to plan with Cloud Code. So for example, if you want to build, let's say, a landing page, now you can allow Cloud Code to run in the plan mode, and now Cloud can plan the entire project.

And afterwards, you can shift to execution, and now it can go and execute and write code based on the original plan. So Cloud is going to break down complex tasks, propose a solution, and iterates on feedback as well. Okay, so here is the Cloud Code agentic workflow. So the first workflow is the exploration phase. Basically what Cloud does first, it reads files and understands your current code base. The second phase is what we call the planning phase, and that's when, let's say, you ask Cloud to build a calorie tracker app, which is one of the apps that we're going to build together. So this is the default, basically, mode. What you could do is, if you

press on the shift and tab, you can toggle between normal mode. You can allow what we call it auto accept. It's just going to go, and I'm going to assume that I'm going to accept anything that Cloud does. The third one is what we call it plan mode, and that's when we basically wanted to plan an entire project initially. And what you'll see that whenever we work on, let's say, a complex project, first we set the Cloud Code to be in the plan mode first, and that will be for Cloud to explore but never edits. And then afterwards, we shift back to the normal mode to actually go and execute the plan. Of course, you can allow auto accept if you wanted to just give Cloud anything, kind of all the rights, and it's going to go and it's going to auto accept anything, basically, that it does. All right, so when to use the plan mode? We use the plan mode when we have multi-file changes where scope is unclear. That means if you are working maybe or starting out on a new project, you don't know fully the scope, so we usually use the plan mode initially.

And when we are trying to explore unfamiliar code base safely. When to skip it? lectures.title: Why Agents and Claude folders containing the same skill.md
lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. I got asked that question a lot, so I just wanted to quickly clarify the confusion. So if you remember, when we installed our front end design skill, what you notice is on the left-hand side here, if you remember, I created that folder, which was build a business front page with skills. Inside that folder, I had two folders created, right? I had the agents, and I also had Claude as well. You're probably wondering, if you actually open them, you will find that they have also the skill.md file included in two locations.

Why that confusion? Well, so I included kind of a summary here of why this is happening. So when you install a skill, two folders have been created to serve kind of different purposes. So we have one that is specific to Claude. So our Claude code, when it wanted to leverage one of these skills, like the front end design skill, it's actually going to use or go to that Claude folder. And simply when you run Claude in your terminal via the CLI, or the command line interface, which is simply what we were typing there here on the bottom, it reads skills from this folder.

But let's assume, for example, that I have another AI agent. Let's say one from Gemini, for example. And please know that within VS Code, you can actually run other agents too. So the idea here is we're going to create another folder. We called it agents. And think of it as more of a generic one. So think of this also as an emerging standard for other AI agents and tools. So for example, if you have, let's say, other applications, let's say Cursor or Windsurf, and if you're running maybe a different AI model outside of Claude, this is going to be kind of the new standard.

And now when these agents want to go and actually create maybe something there, we want to make sure that they also have access to the same skill. And that's why there are two folders there that have been created. And both of them reference the exact same skill. Long story short, again, it's not going to make any difference for us. But just I got asked that question a lot, so I just wanted to clarify it. So both of them, they actually point at the same skill.md file.

So the skill is identical, one that is going to be used by Claude Code, and the other, think of it as more of a generic one, just in case if you plan to use another agent or maybe you plan to use another, as well, development tool, for example, maybe like Cursor. In that folder, now it's not going to go to Claude. It's actually going to go to the agents folder, and it's going to have the access to the exact same skill. All right, that's pretty much all I want you to know.

And that's all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it, and see you in the next one.

lectures.title: Claude Code Plugins
lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. In this video, I wanted to share what do we mean by Cloud Plugins. So let's go ahead and get started. If you remember, we have already covered Cloud Skills. And Skills are simply a markdown file that summarizes a skill that Cloud agents can leverage. And what Anthropic did, which I think is incredibly smart, is the idea of going beyond a skill to include what we call it a plugin. So let me share a quick example.

Let's assume that you work in finance. And let's assume that you do data analysis, for example. So the idea is, let's assume that we have a junior financial analyst coming in, joining, let's say, a company. So for the financial analyst, simply what we do is we give them, or we assume that they have skills. And it's not just one skill. Maybe they have Python programming skills. They know Excel. They know how to create PowerPoint presentations. And they know how to do, let's say, pandas or any of the Python libraries.

So it's not just one skill. Now the new onboarding junior analyst, they have a bundle of skills. What they also need, that they need access to tools. So I need to give them a new Gmail, let's say, account for the company. They also need to have, let's say, access to their calendars, access to Slack, Teams, and so on. And we can give here the agent basically all of that using what we call it MCP, or Model Context Protocol, where we have a standard way for the agent to talk to all of these different tools.

What I need as well to give that junior analyst is, well, I want to give them workflows. I want to tell them, OK, this is how we run the business. What we do is we get the data, let's say, from this source. And then we run a data visualization on it. And then we build dashboards. And we are automating. lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. In this video, I wanted to share a few critical information around context management. So let's go ahead and get started. So first of all, what do we even mean by context and context window? Well, a context window is the total amount of text Cloud can process in a single session. So let me remind you the idea, the idea that we have a large language model, or an LLM, and think of it as it's like a digital brain.

So our brain has billions of neurons. These neurons fire and talk to each other with electrical and chemical signals. It allows us to see, think, and make decisions. And the idea here is, with an LLM, like Opus 4.6, is we just created a brain similar to ours, but it's a digital one. And the idea that you feed in a prompt, let's say I generate this sample code, for example, and what the LLM is going to do, it is going to generate an output for you.

And that's the idea. You give it an input. You prompt it. It's going to generate an output. So the idea is, well, can you feed it in, let's say, 10,000 documents, for example? Or you can feed it in maybe with one document. And that's the idea of what we call it a context window. These LLMs can process a certain fixed amount of information at once. And that's what we call it context window. And it's measured in tokens. So everything counts, your messages, Claude's replies, files it opened, and also all the tools used, all of that is being utilized and is actually consuming some of your context window.

So the problem is when a session exceeds that limit, it's a problem because now Claude doesn't fully understand the entire context because it used its full 1 million context window. So what happened is all the content gets dropped and Claude can no longer reference it. And it's a big problem. So what do we include in a context window? First, it includes the system prompt. So these LLMs, or large language models, they have a system prompt. This has been developed by Anthropic.

And it basically gives Claude general instructions of what to do. And this is, think of it as Anthropic's built-in rules. For example, Anthropic tweaked the LLM not to talk politics, for example, and so on. And this is included as part of, of course, it's training data. It's part of the guardrails in the model. And it's also part of the system prompt as well. We don't have much control over this. But this is already consuming some of the context window.

The second piece of information, it includes information about the tools that it can use. Of course, we have what we call tools via MCP, or Model Context Protocol. And these tools, information about it's actually consuming some of my context window as well. What we include, we include memory too. So these are resources that are persistent across sessions. And they auto grows as Claude learns your project too. What we also have, which is really important, we have that Claude.md file, if you remember.

This actually is being embedded as part of our context window. That's why in the previous video, I told you we need to be super ultra careful with what we include in there because this is persistent across every single run in our project. And that's why we don't use it to dump all the documentation in our Claude.md because we write that and we can control it. And this is what we call it our project instructions. What we have as well is all the messages, all the history that we're feeding in back and forth, also is being recorded too.

And it's included here as well. So the idea is, well, we might easily run out of our context window. And that's why context management is super important. lectures.title: AI Agents 101
lectures.text:
Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video, I'm going to cover the fundamentals of AI agents, so let's go ahead and get started. So what is an AI agent? Well, AI agents are intelligent systems that take a goal, they are going to plan a series of steps, it's going to autonomously execute those steps, it's going to leverage tools and knowledge with minimal human input. Let me show you a practical example. Here I got an AI agent, and of course we have used already Cloud Code, which is an agentic coding tool, and what we did is we asked Cloud, could you please build me an app, right? And now Cloud used tools, it wrote code, it basically created its own subtasks, and now you ended up with the app being built for you. And that's the idea, you can just simply talk to these AI agents and you can tell them, plan my three-day trip to Paris.

What the agent is going to do, it's going to be powered by a large language model or an LLM behind the scenes, this could be GPT models, could be Cloud models, or could be open source models, like let's say DeepSeek for example. And what's going to happen is that first these LLMs, they have planning capability, so now they can create their own subtasks for example. They also have memory, so now they can recall previous preferences from users, so for example they can know, okay, maybe this user, they like museums for example. They also have access to tools, so now they can search, let's say the web, they can look for maps, they can look for hotels, they can also check weather information as well. What we have too is within those agents, we can also have guardrails, so for example they can know that I should suggest only safe suggestions to humans, so I shouldn't give them like, you know, like wrong information, I should not talk politics or maybe religion, and these are what we call them guardrails when we design those agents. And then finally we have what we call it handoffs, so we as humans, we love specialization. So if you go to a company, you will find let's say that you have software engineer, you have electrical engineer, you have human resources,

you also have sales, marketing teams. We don't just hire one person to do everything for us. Why? Because we like specialty, and that's the same idea here. We can have, instead of having one agent, we can have a team or an army of AI agents, and these agents can do handoff, that means they can take a task and they can hand off that task to another AI agent. So for example, this agent here can pass a task to let's say a restaurant booking agent, and now what you get at the end, you get a full itinerary, everything is booked for you, and that's the idea of an AI agent in a nutshell.

It's an LLM that can use its own memory, it can leverage tools, it can actually do action, it can come back, observe what happened, and it can do that loop multiple times, and that's the idea of AI agents in a nutshell. Please note that we are going to learn how to use cloud code to build these agents for us without really knowing much coding, and that's the power of what we will build together today. With that, that's all I have for this video, I hope you enjoyed it, and see you in the next one.

Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. In this video, I'm going to share a few foundations when it comes to building those AI agents. OK, so as we mentioned before, what is an agent? An AI agent is a system that uses a large language model, or an LLM, as its reasoning engine to autonomously plan, take actions, and adapt based on feedback to accomplish goals. So the idea that when ChatGPT was released back in 2022, it was just a basic chatbot.

It's just an LLM, or a large language model. You prompt it, you talk to it in plain English, it just gives you a response, and that's it. And really, what is happening behind the scenes, it is just an auto-completion engine. You just give it an input, like what is the capital of, let's say, France, and then try to predict the next most probable world. It's going to be, let's say, Paris, for example. It didn't have access to external tools, it doesn't have persistent memory, and it's a stateless interaction.

So the LLM on its own is just an auto-completion engine. But now, what you could do is you can take that LLM just as the base brain, and now we can augment it. You can basically power it and make it an AI agent. So now you can take that LLM, and now the LLM can have additional capabilities. So now it can plan multi-step workflows. You can give it access to tools. So now you can give it access to APIs, for example. It can go and search the web. It has access to Google, for example, search.

It can also have the ability to use tools to generate Python code and run Python code, and maybe take a look at the output of that code and take a look at it and maybe come with another action. And that's the idea. Now we have an LLM as the base, and now it can reason, it can think, it can take action, come back, and it can do that multiple iterations. And we found that now these agents can work for 14 hours with a 50% success rate, which is insane.

And of course, maybe by the time you're watching this video, well, this has been like a solved problem, and now you can achieve that almost with 100% accuracy. So it can retain and remember information. And finally, we have the ability for the agents to observe. So now it can take an action. It can observe what it did and come back and forth multiple times. Please note that I showed you already a demo of the Cloud Code and Cloud, actually, web extension taking action and booking basically trips for us, if you remember.

Okay, so let me walk you through a quick walkthrough to fully understand a few additional concepts here that is gonna be useful when we go and build AI agents with Cloud Code. Okay, let's assume that I have an AI agent that all it does, it gives me weather insights. For example, so here I got the AI agent and here what we do is we add what we call it a system prompt to the agent. Basically, we tell the agent who you are, right? So we give it, think of it as a persona.

So for example, I can say you are an assistant that helps users with questions about weather. Instructions, if the user asks about weather, use the weather tool, ask the user for additional details if the request is unclear. So this is what we call it a system prompt. So we can tell the agent, okay, that's who you are. You are, let's say, a data scientist or maybe you are a specialized doctor, for example, or maybe you are a financial analyst and so on.

We'll give it a background information and we call that system prompt. Please note that this is different from what we call it the user prompt. The user prompt is when I actually go as a user and start talking to it. System prompt, think of it as it's a pre-installed software persona that we give to the AI agent. So what I could do here, I can have a user and the user is gonna type here a user prompt. What is the weather today, okay? So you're asking a question.

So because this agent has access to memory, it's actually gonna go and try to see, to get the weather information, I need to know the location, like is he or she, let's say in Sydney, Australia, or maybe Toronto, Canada.

I need to know to give them the weather information. So what it's going to do, it's actually going to check the memory, okay? And it's going to check, kind of perform retrieval first. lectures.text:
Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video I'm going to cover the fundamentals of MCP or Model Context Protocol. Please note that we covered this kind of briefly when we touched around the cloud code and how it uses MCP as well to talk to let's say Gmail, Calendar and so on. But here I just wanted to cover kind of what is actually going on behind the scenes because it's going to be critical for us when we build our AI agents. So MCP is an open standard and open source framework that has been introduced by Anthropic to try to standardize how AI models interact with tools or with the outside world. So think of an MCP protocol, this is simply the logo for MCP, as the USB-C port. It's like this port that I have here.

So basically if something, like if you have let's say a device that supports this USB-C port, you can just plug and play, no questions asked. Why? Because it's a standard and that's the idea here. Beforehand, let me show you the problem first. Before MCP we had an AI agent, let's say you have a Lama model by Meta or maybe you have Anthropic here models like Cloud or maybe have open AI models. And let's assume that these AI models, they need to talk to let's say Gmail or maybe Slack or maybe Google Calendar for example. So every time that these agents need to talk to these tools, we need to have a custom API. So now I need to go make sure that everything is updated, there is you know like a customized way of talking to the outside world. And that was really challenging because well what if Slack updated the way that we talk to Slack for example API. And that's of course a big issue because we didn't have the standard, we didn't have the common unified way for AI agents to talk to the world. And that's when MCP came into play and the idea is I have these AI agents and here I got Gmail, Slack and let's say Google Calendar. And now I can have a unified way. We're using MCP. If any of these services or any of these tools support Model

Context Protocol or MCP, that's amazing. Now I can just allow any AI agent to talk to any of these services using that unified protocol or MCP for short. And now that means I have a standardized API. So please note that MCP has become the industry standard and this was the main blog post that was released by Anthropic. And that was a really power move I would say because it solidified Anthropic as a key player in the market because it became a standard. That means everyone is using MCP now. And you can see here for example that if you go ahead and click on this link, it's going to show you the article here introducing the Model Context Protocol and that was released back in November of 2024. Okay, so let me show you a quick real world application. So assume that we have a simple AI agent that utilizes let's say a currency conversion tool. So for example here I got a tool which is let's say a currency converter tool that is running and it is actually allowing us to talk to this tool via MCP. Okay, and let's assume that me here as a client I'm making a request, I'm asking a large language model like let's say Claude to tell me okay what is a thousand dollars USD in Canadian dollars. I just want to see the conversion, the equivalent. So what the LLM is going to do,

it is going to use Model Context Protocol or MCP to basically use the tool. So because this tool already supports MCP, it's just a way of communicating between the LLM and the tool is quite easy. And here I mentioned that MCP is an open protocol that is designed to be a standard way for models first to discover and interact with tools. It's like a universal plug adapter for AI tools and simply what you get is now you get the Canadian equivalent which is let's say 1,300 Canadian dollars as an example. With that, that's all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it and see you in the next one.

Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video, I'm going to cover an introduction to OpenAI Agents SDK, so let's go ahead and get started. So what is OpenAI Agents SDK? It's a lightweight, Python-first, open-source framework released by OpenAI quite recently, in March of 2025, for building agentic AI applications with very few abstractions. So the idea is that to build AI agents, OpenAI made it extremely easy for us to define an agent, to call an agent, to define the system-level instructions, and I'm going to show you how incredibly easy that is. Please note that this is not a coding course or an agentic AI course, the idea is I want to show you basically how it works from a very high level, and then how to automate it afterwards with cloud code. This is the plan, okay? So if you don't come from a coding background, don't worry, just follow along with me, get an idea of what is going on, and then I'm going to show you how to prompt cloud code, how to get the right skill to automate the entire workflow for you. So first of all, a few additional features is that it has very few primitives. We call them building blocks. That means it is extremely easy to learn. It also works out of the box with room to customize. It also provides what we call an LLM agnostic

framework, meaning that you can use OpenAI Agents SDK with other LLMs or large language models. So for example, if you want to use maybe like Cloud or maybe use, let's say, Gemini, you will be able to use OpenAI Agents SDK and just remove the brain, remove the LLM, and just replace it with any other LLM. As we speak right now, the OpenAI Agents SDK can support 100 plus LLMs, and we need Python 3.1 at least required, 3.10 required. Okay, so here are the core primitives of building AI agents using OpenAI Agents SDK. What I mean by primitives is just building blocks, right? So the first building block, which is obviously the most important one, is what we call it agents. So to define an agents, I can use a building block. We call it agents. I need to specify what model to use, what is the system prompt. I'm going to show you the code. It's going to be incredibly easy for you to understand. Simply, it's an LLM. It's kind of the core building block.

It's an LLM with instructions, tools, handoffs, and also a structured output as well. We also have tools, right? So now I can define a tool, and I can make that tool available to the agent. So it allows me to basically fetch data, run code, and call external APIs. We also have handoffs as one of the core primitives. If you remember, instead of having one agent do the entire task for us, I can have a team of AI agents that work together to try to achieve a task. So that means handoffs, meaning we can have an agent that can delegate one of the tasks to a different AI agent. We also have guardrails. That means guardrails enable you to do checks and validation. That means I can add a guardrail to the agent, tell it, okay, please don't talk politics, or maybe don't mention anything related to, let's say, religion, for example. lectures.title: Build a Team of AI Agents
lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this project. In this project, we are going to take our agentic AI capability, take over to the next level. If you remember, in the previous project, we learned how to build just one simple AI agent with memory. We added the SQLite here session, if you remember. We also used Cloud Code to automate the process for us. So what if I wanted to have not just one AI agent, but maybe a team of AI agents that can do an entire workflow for me?

What you also notice is that in the previous project, we did not leverage any tools. So the agent really did not have access to the outside world. It only retained information through the SQLite session memory. Okay, so here's the plan. In this project, we're going to build a team of AI agents that work together to achieve a goal. So the first agent is going to be a researcher AI agent. And here, we are going to leverage a super powerful API. We call it Tavli Search.

And Tavli is widely used, and it's incredibly powerful. And it's also free for a limited number of requests. So you can go ahead and use it without paying any API costs for the API. So what I'm going to do is I'm going to prompt the researcher AI agent with a topic. The agent's going to leverage Tavli. It's going to come back with a ton of research results. And these are going to be our research findings here. And instead of just presenting these results directly to the user, I'm going to have another AI agent.

And that will be an analyst AI agent that is going to take all these different results from the researcher. It's going to perform an analysis basically for it. It's going to perform analysis and key insights. And then I'm going to have another agent, and that will be a writer AI agent that's going to take the analysis from this one, and it's going to basically write an entire full report for me. And the idea here is we're not going to be using one AI agent.

We can have a team of agents that work together in a predefined workflow. And the idea is I'm going to have a manager function that manages everything for us end to end. So the idea is we're going to invoke the researcher agent. The outcome is going to be fed to an analyst. The analyst is going to analyze the results, have some sort of deep reasoning in there, and then is going to pass along the results to the writer agent to write the report for me.

Okay, so please note that the API that we're going to use is what we call the Tavli API. And Tavli allows developers to connect AI agents to the web. It is simply used for real-time search, extraction, research, and web crawling as well through a single secure API. So you're probably wondering, okay, why are we even using Tavli? Well, Tavli is incredibly powerful, and you can actually see that here from that graph. Basically, you'll see Google SERP, which is another API powered by Google.

It has an accuracy of almost 82%, while Tavli has an accuracy of almost 93%. It's also free to use for a limited number of requests. So this is great. So now we can go and test it out. You can also see here when it comes to latency that Tavli is actually ultra-fast compared to other APIs as well. If you go ahead and click on that link, that is going to direct you to our Tavli here. And this is simply the Tavli official website. It's basically telling you that now you can connect your AI agents to the web.

And you need to sign up here. I already signed up. And of course, you need to get an API key. So let me log in and let me show you what or how to get the API key because we will need that. So let me log in. So here we go. So now I logged in into my account. You need to sign up, of course. And what you see here is on the left-hand side, you should see the API playground if you want to play with it. And you can see here the API keys. You can just click plus, and you can give it here a key.

So I'm going to call it, for example, let's say the agentic AI, let's say Cloud Code because this is simply what we're doing here. And then I'm going to say create. And I'm going to be or to see an API key basic that has been created. And here we go. Now we should see that this is simply the key here. You can just copy that. And that's pretty much it. We are going to need it later on when we go and use our Tavli search API. OK, so this is the first point.

The second point is I wanted to share what we call it a Pydantic library. And basically, we use Pydantic to generate a structured output from these LLMs or AI agents. So Pydantic is a Python library that is used to validate and parse data using what we call it Python type hints. So the idea is I wanted to have the, let's say, writer agent generate an output in a certain structure. I wanted it, let's say, to be in a text format. I don't want to generate, let's say, binary outputs, for example.

And that's the idea of Pydantic. I can force the AI agent to generate structured output. And this is really important. Well, why? Because we have agents that depend on each other. If you go back, you will see that this agent, for example, relies on the results from the previous agent. So now I need to use Pydantic to structure simply the output. So now I can pass the output from one agent to the other. And I'm going to show you that in code. Again, don't worry, because we're not going to be writing any code at all.

And basically, you define a data structure using a class. Pydantic is going to ensure the data is correct, the types, required fields, everything is set. It even converts data automatically as well, if possible. And that's really all I wanted to know when it comes to Pydantic. And these are the key learning objectives of our project. First, we're going to create a modular AI agent, not just one, a team. We can have a researcher, we can have an analyst, we can have a writer with specialized roles for information gathering, analysis, and reporting.

We're also going to implement agent collaboration by passing the output from one agent to another in a structured workflow. We're also going to customize AI agent behavior by rewriting instructions to adapt outputs to specific language or formats. And finally, we're going to build our manager function that is going to orchestrate the entire workflow for us. With that, that's pretty much all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it. In the next video, let me walk you through the code first inside of a Jupyter notebook.

And of course, automate the whole thing using Cloud Code in the following video. With that, that's all I have. I hope you enjoyed it and see you in the next one.

lectures.title: The Karpathy Wiki Pattern
lectures.text:
Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video, I wanted to quickly share what do we mean by the Karpathy wiki pattern. So let's go ahead and get started. So I assume a lot of you know who he is. He is Andrei Karpathy. He is, as I mentioned, one of the top AI voices in the world. And the idea is, and this was basically came out of his GitHub page as well. Instead of just retrieving from raw documents at query time, what we want is we want a large language model or an LLM to incrementally build and maintain a persistent wiki. The idea, as I mentioned, is going to be a personal Wikipedia that includes pages about you, about your business, who you talk to. And the idea is that wiki is going to compound every time and it kept current. So you don't have to explain to the agent every time you talk to what you do, what your goals are, what is your brand. All of that information is captured in a personal wiki. And the beautiful thing is that it is maintained autonomously by the AI agent, which is in this example is going to be Cloud Code. So if you are maybe like deep a bit into AI and maybe data science, you're probably wondering, OK, like why don't we just use RAG or retrieval augmented generation? So if you're not familiar with RAG, basically the idea is

you can have an LLM and then you can have a knowledge base. And then before you send a prompt to the LLM, you're going to retrieve some information from that database and then you're going to augment the prompt with the information retrieved and then you're going to feed it to the LLM. This is what we call it retrieval augmented generation. I'm going to include additional slides in the appendix if you would like to check it out if you're interested. But don't worry, we're not going to cover RAG, I would say, in great detail or anything here. But this is just an important distinction between our Wikipedia or personal wiki that we are building now versus RAG. So with RAG, what you do is simply you upload files, let's say about your business, and then this data is going to be divided into chunks. And then the agent is going to start to retrieve some information from that database. So LLM is going to rediscover knowledge from scratch with every question.

And this is the challenge with RAG, right? Every time you're going to talk to it, the agent has to go, it's going to start to grab information from that database. And simply, it doesn't compound over time. It doesn't learn over time. It doesn't get smarter over time. So there is no accumulation over time of information and knowledge. Also, multi-document questions require repiecing of multiple fragments. And if you have used Notebook LLM or maybe like ChatGPT as well, this simply approach is applied everywhere.

You are building a custom GPT or maybe an AI agent inside of Copilot. This is basically the idea, the use RAG behind the scenes. So what's powerful about the idea of a personal wiki is now the large language model is going to build a persistent compounding artifact. So it compounds over time. As new sources are integrated into existing pages, every page is going to have a tag associated with it. And now, basically, the agent will be able to connect the dots. Basically, it's going to know, okay, my goal is to, let's say, I hope to, let's say, teach a 1 million student one day. I listed that goal before. So this is going to be tagged as one of the goals. So for example, when I asked the agent, what I should do, let's say, what I should post, for example, and the agent is going to link that to my goals. And the post is going to be related, or at least the agent, when it comes out with content, it's going to put that goal in there. And all the advice, all the email write-ups, all the artifacts generated by the agent, it's going to be tied by that page, by that goal.

And it also has the proper tag associated with it as well. The wiki, in simple terms, gets richer with every source added. All right. So when it comes to the wiki architecture, there is generally three layers. The first one is the raw sources. This is simply the curated source of truth. The idea is the agent is not allowed to make any changes in here. Think of it that I'm going to upload, for example, my resume. I don't want the agent to go and start creating a new resume. I'm just going to keep that. And that would be the raw sources of truth.

So you can also include articles. You can include papers, images, data files. This is immutable. That means the agent can't or never modifies it. That would be the core part of our wiki. The second piece, well, the actual wiki, and that's the agent has full control, read and write access over it. This is the LLM generated knowledge pages. It includes summaries. It includes entity pages, concept pages. The LLM owns this layer entirely. And it will be able to also establish links between all these pages as well. And finally, we need a schema, right?

We need to think of it as a playbook. And that playbook is included inside the cloud.md. Simply, it tells the large language model how the wiki is structured and what works as well when we actually go ahead and run it. And please note that if that's not clear so far, don't worry, because I'm actually going to open next our personal wiki. I'm going to show you a few examples that will blow your mind away, okay? So in a nutshell, raw sources, the agent is not allowed to read and write from them, like your CV, for example. The wiki, the agent has full control over it. It's going to establish also all the links. And the schema, think of it as this is the operating system, how the agent is going to structure the wiki and also establish all the connections between the pages. Okay. So why this works? Hello everyone and welcome to this video. In this video, I wanted to share some of the slash commands that comes readily available for you when you get the personal OS folder. Some of these slash commands are as follows. Under the .clod slash commands, you will find basically these automated workflows that have been created already for you. The most important one of all is well, the setup because that's actually what we are going to run in the next videos.

We're just going to say slash setup. This is an automated already slash command that I created. The idea is when you say slash setup, it's going to tell you this is going to be the first run onboarding. It's going to install the skills for you. If you remember, I need the PowerPoint skill, I need the Excel skill. It's going to build the identity as well of the agent, it's going to configure the brand, and it's going to initialize the vault and the notion pages as well.

Well, what if I wanted to create a new automation? For example, I want to create an automation that performs, let's say, CRM or Customer Relationship Management, for example. I would like to keep a database that tracks all my customers and all their e-mails, for example, and I want to place that in notion. Well, to create a new automation, we just say slash new, and that is going to create a new automation for us, including a Cloud.MD that is specific to this automation.

It captures, think of it as the playbook specific for this automation. Please note that this is going to be different from the master Cloud.MD. The idea is we have multiple levels of Cloud.MD. We have one in the root directory, and that's think of it as it's an onboarding for us, for what we do, for what the agent does basically for you specifically, general information. In each of these simply automations, we're going to have Cloud.MD file. Don't worry about it if you are a bit confused about that, because when we actually go and run these automations, I'm going to walk you through the multiple levels of Cloud.MD so you can get an idea of what's included in there.

Well, what if I wanted to get a status, for example, from the agent? I can just say slash status. It's going to tell me what is happening, what are the recent runs, the project progress, and all the upcoming tasks as well that the agent is going to do. Well, what if I wanted to, let's say, ingest information from my CV or maybe from LinkedIn and place all that data in the vault? Well, you can just say slash ingest, and that is going to do all of that for you.

It's going to process raw sources into Wiki pages, and it's going to keep track of links, extract people and companies as well. Well, what if you wanted to, let's say, check that vault health? You can just say slash lint, and that is going to check the vault health, and it's going to check for orphans pages, for maybe like broken links and so on. And what if I wanted to, let's say, set up a new brand configuration, maybe in the future? You could just say slash brand, and that is going to set up or refresh the brand config based on the new templates or logos that you placed in there.

If you're wondering where are these slash commands, let me show you. So if you go back to the Visual Studio code, if you remember, we didn't run anything at all, really. All we did is we just copied that personal OS folder, that one that is included in the course package. I started VS Code. I set file, open folder. I directed it to that folder. And here, what you notice is inside that dot clod, here we got all these slash commands, basically, all these markdown files.

So one of them is, for example, let's say here's the setup, which is what we're going to run next. Basically, the idea is here, it includes all the steps about how to set up your personal AI agent. So now, instead of going there and trying to figure out, okay, like, what do I need to set up the agent? You just say slash setup, and that's it. And then basically the cloud code's going to walk you through the steps. From a very high level, basically what we're doing is, first, it's going to guide the user through setting up the personal OS.

Step one, I need to install the skills, right? So here you'll see, I'm going to install the skills for cloud office skills. You also see some of skills here related to PowerPoint as well. What you do next is you want it to check all the connections. So we want to make sure that the Gmail is connected, the Notion is connected, and also the calendar is connected. I want to build the identity. So here, I'm just going to ask the user, basically, when we run it, do you need to place your own data or just keep the default values for the brand?

Let's keep going. You will also notice that I need to ingest data, right? So I'm going to ask you, that will be the first step coming up next, is to place your resume inside of that inbox folder. So this is going to be the raw data that the agent is going to extract, basically, all the information about your LinkedIn profile, about what your job, what you do, and it's going to ingest that data, and it's going to fill up your vault and also your sole.md file as well.

Let's keep going. So it's going to go through the setup here for the brand. It's going to do all the data ingestion. It's going to write your sole.md. Again, don't worry about it. It's already pre-built for you. So really, I know it might be a bit overwhelming because there are so many things happening, but all I want you to know for now is, well, what we have done is we just got the personal OS, unzip it, put in the desktop, VS Code. You direct it there.

I'm going to show you in the next module how to establish the connections, connectors, run slash setup, and everything will going to be built for you. It's going to be incredibly fun coming up next. Here, we're talking about the index and log, and let's keep going. And after we are done, basically, we need to see these 10 automations. If you remember, I have 10 automations that we plan to run. For example, we have research team. We have email triage.

We have expense wrangler. I'm going to walk them through it again next, but this is simply just a summary of our setup slash command. And please note that there are so many other slash commands that are available here as well. With that, that's all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it, and I will see you in the next one.

sections.title: Setup Your Personal AI Agent in Claude Code & Cowork

lectures.title: Overview of the Personal AI Agent Setup Process
lectures.text:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to this video. In this video, we are going to set up our personal AI agent. We're going to learn how to create our Vault. And also, we will learn how to connect Obsidian 2 to visualize the Vault. So it's going to be incredibly fun to watch. So let's go ahead and get started. So let me recap what did we cover in the previous module, and also show you a quick intro to our personal AI agent setup. So when it comes to the architecture, at a glance, if you remember, you, you're going to be typing commands in Cloud Code.

We are going to use Cloud Code, of course, going to be connected to all our connectors, like Gmail, connected to Notion, connected to our calendar as well via MCP. Basically, we're going to have our personal OS, if you remember, personal operating system, inside of it, inside that folder structure, we had our Cloud.md file, think of it as the onboarding information to the agent. And, of course, we have the personality and goals in the Soul.md. And finally, of course, we had that memory in the Vault about me, about people that I interact with, about meetings, and about the business as well.

And, of course, when you run that, you just get outputs, like in PowerPoint format, in emails, you get email drafts, and you also get final reports in your brand as well. Let me recap as well a few of the key design patterns, if you remember, we had the Carpathian wiki, the idea that we have three layers, we have the sources, these are immutable, that means the agent is not allowed to, let's say, modify my CV, for example, we had the wiki, the agent can do whatever they want with it, and we also had the schema that simply connects all these different wiki or pages, and it also shows you the relationships between them too.

We also have the voice of the agent is inside of Soul.md file, automation blueprints, if you remember, we're going to have 10 automation blueprints, and brand protocol, all the brands are included, the brand details are included in that brand folder, if you remember, you also have the post-run ingestion, so after every run, the agent is going to extract all the details about, let's say, the meetings that I attended, and extract people who I interacted with, and basically update the vault, so now it grows and learns as we move along.

And finally, which is super powerful, and it helped me personally a lot, the idea of self-correction, when the agent makes mistakes, well, it's going to log that error to make sure that we're not going to make that mistake ever again. Okay, we covered all of that in great detail before, this is just a quick recap. Please note that for our personal agent, we're going to have three MCP connections. The first one is going to be Gmail, so we will be able to read data from our Gmail account, please note that you can also connect it to Microsoft 365, because I got asked that question a lot, and that will be the first piece.

Of course, we need to connect it to our Google Calendar as well, so now we can list events, we can create meetings, invites as well, and it can, basically, the agent can list all the upcoming events, it can create or update meetings, and also find available time slots as well. Please note that OpenCLAW is a bit different from CLAW code with dispatch mode. Anthropic basically tries to keep some sort of guardrails, because again, all these agents are really still in an experimental phase, right?

So what they did is that they don't allow you to talk, for example, to dispatch, and send an email right away. It can create a draft for you, but you still need to be, as a human, in the loop, be involved to click Send. Please note that this is as we speak today, this might change in the future, but kind of Anthropic wanted to have some sort of reliability there. Just imagine if you are an enterprise, and this agent starts to send emails everywhere, and maybe these emails are, some of them, if it's not set up properly, could be an AI slop.

It's just going to be an absolute mess. So that's why it allows you to have a human in the loop just to kind of agree or deny a draft email. We also have a notion, right? So the agent will be able to create pages, create databases, manage tasks, and of course, will be able to create a sprint board to manage all the 10 automations, think of it as a program manager, basically, agent, that would allow to move all these different tasks from, let's say, to do, to done, for example.

We'll learn how all of that coming up next. Okay. Please note that really all I'm going to do next, and I'm going to show you that in the next video, I'm going to direct Cloud Code to work inside the personal OS folder. I need to keep my resume up to date, and I want you to create your resume as well. And I also wanted to show you the document that we are going to prep together. It's going to come up next too. We're going to list all the goals, all the information in there about you, about links to your social media, for example.

And when we run the setup, this is what's going to happen behind the scenes. Basically, the agent is going to install all the skills needed. It's going, such as PowerPoint and Excel. It's going to test your Gmail calendar and notion. It's going to build your identity. So it's going to ask smart questions simply about you. And it's going to set up the brand. So it's going to extract all the brand colors, all the logos, and so on. And it's going to update, if you remember, that brand config file, .md file.

It's going to ingest to wiki. So it's going to extract data from your resume and from your goals and simply put it in the sole.md. And also update the vault with all the wiki pages. It's going to initialize Notion. So basically, which is, I think it's going to be mind-blowing, to watch Cloud Code making changes directly to your Notion board. So it's just going to go create a board. It's going to start creating a Kanban board inside of Notion. And then you will be able to, as I asked you in the previous few videos, to install Obsidian.

And you will be able to direct Obsidian to work directly inside the vault. So you'll be able to visualize all your knowledge base, all the information. And as you interact with the agent, you will find that this knowledge starts to grow as you interact with it. Okay? So with getting started, first, I want you to install Cloud Code. I'm assuming that you have done that in the past so many times. Make sure that you have installed Obsidian. This is really important, and I also showed you how to do that before.

We are going to authenticate MCPs, which is going to come up next. We'll learn how to connect to our Gmail, Calendar, and Notion. After you do that, you just run the setup, and then we're going to start building together. With that, that's all I have for this video. I hope you enjoyed it. Now it's the fun time. Let's go back, let's open Cloud Code, and let's build our personal AI agent together. Please stay tuned, best of luck, and I will see you in the next video.

Okay so please note that in the PowerPoint slides I included a screenshot of every step along the way so just in case maybe if you wanted to go back reference the slides I took screenshots of every step just to keep it as simple as possible for you. So the first step is as I mentioned we need to run our slash setup and you will be asked to place your data inside your inbox folder. So basically what I want you to do is I want you to set up two documents. The first one is going to be a sample resume and the second one is going to be a document that includes all your social media links, all your goals, your agent personality and also sample write-ups. So let me show you what that data looks like. Please note that I included a sample of this data so just in case if you would like let's say to take my sample here and modify it for you you can go ahead and do that. Here I included a sample of my resume for example of course you can just replace this entirely with your resume. Okay I tried to keep it as detailed as possible basically here but you don't have to just two pages would be should be good

enough. The most important document is this document here. Okay so in this document basically I outlined all the information that the agent need to know about me. So first of all I included links to the social media. The first one is going to be the LinkedIn page and I would love to connect with each and every one of you so you can just click on that link it's going to take you to my LinkedIn page and I would love to also reshare your work as well if you want to have more visibility.

The second piece is I added the Maven experts page. So for example I teach courses on live cohorts on Maven and this is going to be one of the pages. Let me show you. So if you actually open let's say the LinkedIn page. So this is the sample LinkedIn page. The agent is going to go here it's going to extract all this information so it's going to know a lot more about me about what I care about and so on. So really all you need to do is to replace this with your LinkedIn profile link. Here for example I got the Maven page of course you can replace it let's say if you have a website for example you can just go you can replace this here link with your link as an example and here I also included a link to let's say my YouTube channel for example so this is my YouTube channel I just added a link here so the agent will be able to go know basically what I care about know what kind of videos I published because I'm going to ask the agent in the future to okay can you suggest maybe my next YouTube video or let's say create a content plan for me so well the beautiful thing the agent knows who I am right because it knows my YouTube video it can go there it can scan all the videos that I posted as well in the past and it can also
